The study used 2024-T3 clad aluminum panels measuring 381 × 89 × 1.6 mm with a 25.4 mm central crack.
Octagonal single-sided boron/epoxy composite patches with 5 and 6 plies were designed and tested.
Patch thickness per ply was 0.132 mm, with adhesive thickness of 0.18 mm using FM-73 adhesive.
Stiffness ratios of 1.14 (5-ply) and 1.38 (6-ply) were calculated for patch to skin stiffness.
Finite element analysis used 8-noded hexagonal elements with 24 degrees of freedom.
Uniaxial tensile loading of 0.279 GPa (40.5 ksi) was used for design, with fatigue loading at 0.093 GPa (13.5 ksi) for 150,000 cycles.
Maximum skin stress decreased significantly after patch application.
Stress concentration shifted from crack front in unpatched panels to patch edges in repaired panels.
Tapering patch edges reduces peel stresses and secondary bending moments.
Adhesive thickness affects joint strength; thin layers (0.124–0.249 mm) are optimal.
Adhesive with high shear modulus improves joint strength but ultimate shear strain is more critical.
Patch thickness should balance stiffness to avoid early yielding due to neutral axis shift.
Fatigue crack growth rate follows Paris law and is reduced by patch application.
Experimental tensile tests validated finite element analysis results.
CRAS software facilitated patch design and parameter optimization.
Composite patch repair extends structural life and restores load carrying capacity.
Adhesively bonded patches avoid corrosion and stress concentrations associated with mechanical fasteners.
The study confirms the US Air Force interest in composite patch repairs for aging aircraft.
Patch design requires consideration of overlap length, patch thickness, adhesive properties, and tapering.
The maximum permissible strain in boron fibers was limited to 0.005 to avoid fiber breakage.
